abstract: The Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff equations admit singular solutions in which a negative point mass is surrounded by a self-gravitating fluid. For a $\Gamma$-law polytropic equation of state, these solutions, which we call singustars, are thick shells bounded by two zero-pressure surfaces around a naked, repulsive, negative-mass singularity, with a Schwarzschild exterior. They form a two-parameter family, labeled by the mass $M$ and the compactness $C\equiv M/R$. Singustars join regular polytropes as the central negative mass vanishes and reach compactness beyond the Buchdahl bound. From exact equilibria and their radial modes, we find that singustars with $\Gamma = 2$ are stable only for $M\lesssim0.63$ and $C\lesssim0.25$, a region that nonetheless contains configurations more compact than any stable regular polytrope, although none with a light ring. In the numerically resolved parameter space, unstable singustars have a single unstable radial mode; many are energetically unbound. Nonlinear evolutions in ingoing null coordinates show that the end state depends on the perturbation. For the collapsing models studied, backward tracing of outgoing null rays identifies an event-horizon generator with a past endpoint on the singularity, before the first trapped surface appears. Outward perturbations disperse unbound shells and leave the singularity naked, while a bound shell migrates toward, and oscillates about, a stable configuration with the same conserved masses.
hook: Stars built around a negative-mass singularity can be stable and more compact than ordinary ones.

summary: Solutions of the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations describe thick fluid shells around a repulsive negative-mass point. Equilibrium and radial-mode calculations show stable ones for Gamma = 2 when M is below about 0.63 and compactness below about 0.25, and some beat any stable ordinary polytrope. Nonlinear runs show collapse or dispersal depending on the push. These are theoretical objects with no known formation route.
title: Singustars: Between Black Holes and Compact Stars
